reconcile.connective: Commentators resolve the tension by ranking holiness: God is holy essentially and infinitely, while creatures are holy only derivatively, by imitation and sanctification, never equaling him.

discrepancy.connective: The objection is pressed by Steve Wells, who lists this as a contradiction: Revelation's claim that God 'only' is holy cannot, as worded, stand alongside the repeated commands that Israel and the church be holy.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (skepticsannotatedbible.com, 'Is only God holy?')
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013; online ed. skepticsannotatedbible.com)

excerpts.excerpt_text: God is essentially holy: the creature is holy in so far as it is sanctified by God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Distinguishes the two senses of 'holy' directly: God's holiness is essential/intrinsic, the creature's is derived sanctification — the exact distinction that dissolves the 'only God is holy' vs. 'be holy' tension.

excerpts.excerpt_text: for thou only art holy; not only perfectly holy, as man, but infinitely and essentially holy, as God, and the fountain of holiness to his people, as Mediator …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Speaks to the Revelation pole itself: 'thou only art holy' is read as God being holy in a unique, infinite, essential degree and as the source of others' holiness — not a denial that creatures can be holy.

excerpts.excerpt_text: It is required that Israel be a holy people, because the God of Israel is a holy God, Lev 19:2. Their being distinguished from all other people by peculiar laws and customs was intended to teach them a real separation from the world and the flesh, and an entire devotedness to God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Frames the holiness command as imitation that never equals God's own perfect, eternal holiness — a third distinct voice making the same gradient distinction.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Leviticus 19:1-2 and 1 Peter 1:15-16
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this passage directly, harmonizing the command to be holy with God's own holiness by the imitation-without-equality distinction ('we must imitate him, though we can never equal him').
